facts.statement: Robert M. Sullivan described the fossil in 2006, which was found in the summer of 2005 in the Kirtland Formation of New Mexico.
facts.quote: In 2006, Robert M. Sullivan described a left frontal bone found during the summer of 2005 in the Kirtland Formation (De-na-zin Member) of the San Juan Basin in New Mexico, United States.

facts.statement: The specimen was accessioned as SMP VP-1955 at the State Museum of Pennsylvania and was originally assigned to the species Saurornitholestes robustus.
facts.quote: Permanently accessioned as SMP VP-1955 in the State Museum of Pennsylvania in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, United States, Sullivan assigned it to the new species Saurornitholestes robustus.

facts.statement: In 2012, Alan H. Turner considered the taxon a nomen dubium, and in 2014, David C. Evans determined it was an indeterminate troodontid not belonging to Saurornitholestes.
facts.quote: However, Alan H. Turner and colleagues considered this taxon as a possible nomen dubium (dubious name) in 2012, while David C. Evans and colleagues found in 2014 that the specimen actually represented an indeterminate troodontid, and thus was not referrable to the genus Saurornitholestes.

facts.statement: In 2026, Hector E. Rivera-Sylva and colleagues tentatively assigned the specimen to the genus Xenovenator as X.? robustus.
facts.quote: In 2026, Hector E. Rivera-Sylva and colleagues tentatively assigned "S." robustus to their new genus Xenovenator, creating the new combination X.? robustus, based on anatomical characteristics shared with the type species of that genus, X. espinosai.

facts.statement: The name Dinevenator honors the Diné people and the Latin word for hunter.
facts.quote: The generic name, Dinevenator, honors the Diné (or Navajo) people of the American Southwest, where the fossil was found, combined with the Latin word venator, meaning hunter.

facts.statement: Dinevenator lived during the Late Cretaceous (Campanian) age.
The type locality for Dinevenator is the Kirtland Formation.
Dinevenator was found in the United States.
Dinevenator was found in the region of New Mexico.
Dinevenator is an extinct troodontid theropod known from the Late Cretaceous Kirtland Formation of New Mexico.
facts.quote: Dinevenator () is an extinct genus of troodontid theropod dinosaur known from the Late Cretaceous (Campanian age) Kirtland Formation of New Mexico, United States.

facts.statement: Previous research assigned the specimen to the genera Saurornitholestes and Xenovenator.
facts.quote: Previous work had assigned it to the genera Saurornitholestes and Xenovenator.

facts.statement: David C. Evans and colleagues found in 2014 that the specimen represented an indeterminate troodontid and could not be referred to Saurornitholestes.
facts.quote: However, Alan H. Turner and colleagues considered this taxon as a possible nomen dubium (dubious name) in 2012, while David C. Evans and colleagues found in 2014 that the specimen actually represented an indeterminate troodontid, and thus was not referrable to the genus Saurornitholestes.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis recovered Dinevenator robustus as the basal-most taxon in a clade of robust troodontins and as the sister taxon to Albertavenator curriei and Xenovenator espinosai.
It was debated whether the taxon was a nomen dubium or an indeterminate troodontid not belonging to Saurornitholestes.

rejected.statement: In 2026, Steven E. Jasinski and Robert M. Sullivan redescribed the specimen as a distinct genus named Dinevenator.
rejected.quote: Later that year, Steven E. Jasinski and Robert M. Sullivan redescribed SMP VP-1955, reinterpreting it as belonging to a distinct genus, which they named Dinevenator.

rejected.statement: In the 2026 redescription, Dinevenator was placed as the basalmost member of the "robust forms" subclade of Troodontini.
rejected.quote: Dinevenator was placed as the basalmost member of the "robust forms" subclade of Troodontini, rather than as the sister to X. espinosai.
